slides.title: Data: The Foundation
content: Data is a collection of raw facts that lack meaning on their own.
Examples: 100, 250, age, Ethiopia, 010101
Data can be represented in various forms: numbers, text, and images.
One form of representation is better than others depending on the type of data and context.
Key Point: Data must be processed to become useful.

slides.title: Information: Data with Context
content: Information is data that has been processed and organized to provide meaning.
It answers questions like 'who', 'what', 'when', and 'where'.
Example: Daily sales data aggregated by week shows whether sales are increasing.
Information can be represented in tables, line graphs, bar graphs, or formulas.
Key Point: Information is data put into context.

slides.title: Knowledge: Applying Information
content: Knowledge is understanding and skills acquired by integrating information.
It is gained through experience, reading, discussion, and active engagement.
Example: Knowing how to ride a bicycle (information) vs. actually riding it (knowledge).
Knowledge guides our actions and decisions.
Key Point: Knowledge is understanding gained through application.

slides.title: Wisdom: The Highest Level
content: Wisdom is the ability to make sound judgments and wise decisions using knowledge.
It represents the highest level of human understanding.
It involves intuitive, logical, creative, and collective thinking.
Example: Using your knowledge of riding to teach someone else or to adapt to a new type of bike.
Key Point: Wisdom is the best use of knowledge.

slides.title: The DIKW Pyramid
content: Data, Information, Knowledge, and Wisdom form a hierarchical pyramid.
Data is at the bottom, and Wisdom is at the top.
As you move up the pyramid, the value and meaning of the content increase.
Data -> Information -> Knowledge -> Wisdom.
Key Point: The DIKW pyramid illustrates the flow from raw facts to actionable insight.

slides.title: What is an Information System (IS)?
content: An IS is a set of interrelated components working together to collect, process, store, and disseminate information.
It generates different types of reports for organizational tasks.
Example: School information system captures student data from assessments.
This data is summarized to show overall performance, used for ranking and organization.
Key Point: IS is a framework for managing data to support decision-making.

slides.title: Components of an Information System
content: An IS has five major components: Hardware, Software, Data/Information, People, and Procedures.
Hardware: Physical devices (computers, servers, network devices).
Software: Instructions/commands (OS, DBMS, applications).
Data/Information: The critical asset stored and processed.
People: Trained personnel who operate and manage the system.
Procedures: Policies and steps for using and maintaining the system.

slides.title: Example: Human Resource Information System (HRIS)
content: HRIS is a type of IS that manages employee data.
Data stored: Recruitment data, Demographic data (ID, name, DOB, position), Performance records, Training records, Compensation (salary).
Technologies used: Server computers, desktops, laptops, networks.
Software components: Recruitment software, Time and attendance software, Performance management software, Training and development software.
Key Point: HRIS automates and streamlines HR processes.

slides.title: E-Government
content: E-Government uses IS to provide electronic services to citizens.
Goal: Increase efficiency, transparency, and citizen participation.
Example: Ethiopian Ministry of Health portal provides health services to citizens.
Benefits: Establishes trust, facilitates information sharing, allows easy access to government decisions, reduces costs, improves convenience.
Key Point: E-Gov makes government services more accessible and efficient.

slides.title: E-Banking
content: E-Banking is technology-based banking that avoids paper documents.
Services: Internet banking, ATM, mobile banking, credit/debit cards, EFT.
Benefits: Lower cost for banks, 24/7 access for customers, instant transactions, immediate account balance checks.
Challenges: Digital theft, exclusion of digitally illiterate citizens, lack of infrastructure.
Key Point: E-Banking offers convenience and efficiency.

slides.title: E-Learning and E-Commerce
content: E-Learning: Education delivered through digital devices.
Benefits: Flexibility, student-centered learning, access to diverse resources, reduced costs.
Challenges: Physical isolation, less teacher control, technology costs.
E-Commerce: Buying and selling goods and services over the Internet.
Advantages: Avoids intermediaries, convenience, increased bargaining power, global reach.
Key Point: Both services leverage IT for enhanced access and convenience.

slides.title: Telemedicine and Teleconference
content: Telemedicine: Remote healthcare, with caregiver and patient in different locations.
Benefits: Overcomes geographical barriers, reduces costs, access to specialists.
Limitations: Requires technical training and equipment.
Teleconference: Meeting of people from different locations electronically.
Types: Audio conferencing (voice-only) and Video conferencing (voice + images).
Benefits: Saves time and travel costs, can accommodate more people.
Key Point: These services bridge physical distances.

slides.title: IT for Entrepreneurship
content: Entrepreneurship: Designing, launching, and running a new business.
IT is transforming the world of work and creating new opportunities.
IT-enabled businesses: Online training, data entry, internet cafes, online sales.
Benefits: Creates employment opportunities, generates income, diversifies the economy.
Example: RIDE taxi-hailing service in Ethiopia.
Key Point: IT lowers the barrier to starting a business.

slides.title: What is Artificial Intelligence (AI)?
content: AI is a branch of computer science that deals with designing systems that mimic human intelligence.
Examples of human intelligence: Reasoning and generalization.
AI has become powerful due to increased computer capacity and availability of large amounts of data.
Key Point: AI is about creating machines that can think and learn.

slides.title: Branches of AI: Machine Learning & Robotics
content: Machine Learning: Algorithms that allow computers to learn from data and improve themselves.
Applications: Fraud detection, recommendation systems, email spam filters, speech recognition.
Robotics: Study of machines (robots) that substitute human tasks.
Applications: Car manufacturing, handling radioactive wastes, space exploration, household chores (vacuum cleaners).
Key Point: ML enables learning, while Robotics enables physical action.

slides.title: Branches of AI: NLP & Expert Systems
content: Natural Language Processing (NLP): Enables computers to understand human language.
Applications: Spam detection, machine translation (Google Translate), virtual assistants (Siri, Alexa), sentiment analysis, fake news identification.
Expert Systems: Computer programs that emulate human experts.
Components: User Interface, Knowledge Base, Inference Engine.
Example: MYCIN – Expert system for infectious diseases.
Key Point: NLP interprets language, and Expert Systems replicate expert decision-making.

slides.title: Applications of AI (Part 1)
content: Online Shopping: Personalized recommendations.
Autonomous Cars: Self-driving vehicles using GPS, radar, and cameras.
Social Media: Personalized content, targeted advertising, facial recognition.
Surveillance: Real-time detection of suspicious behavior.
Agriculture: Precision farming, pest detection, soil health monitoring.
Key Point: AI is integrated into many daily-use technologies.

slides.title: Applications of AI (Part 2)
content: Customer Service: Chatbots using NLP for support.
Healthcare: Disease diagnosis, drug development, surgical assistance.
Space Exploration: Data processing, mission planning, robot astronauts (Robonaut).
Smart Homes: Home security, automation, smoke alerts.
Banks: Fraud detection in credit card transactions.
Search Engines: Ranking algorithms, understanding user queries.
Key Point: AI's applications are vast and growing.

slides.title: Augmented Reality (AR)
content: AR overlays computer-generated digital data onto the real world.
It blends the real and virtual worlds for an engaging user experience.
Devices: Smartphones, tablets, head-mounted displays, smart glasses.
Example: Capturing an object with a camera and overlaying information about it.
Key Point: AR enhances the real world with digital information.

slides.title: Virtual Reality (VR)
content: VR creates a fully immersive, 3D computer-generated simulated environment.
It replaces the real world with an artificial one.
Devices: Goggles, headsets, gloves, bodysuits.
VR responds to user movements in real-time, creating an illusion of reality.
Key Point: VR replaces the real world with a virtual one.

slides.title: AR vs VR & Applications
content: AR is partially immersive and works in a real-world setting.
VR is fully immersive and operates in a completely virtual world.
Applications in Education: Interactive learning, time travel, concrete visualization.
Applications in Healthcare: Surgical training, tele-surgery, patient distraction.
Applications in Entertainment: Interactive museum visits, immersive cinemas, games.
Key Point: Both AR and VR are transforming education, healthcare, and entertainment.

slides.title: Data Science and Big Data
content: Data Science: An interdisciplinary field using tools, algorithms, and machine learning to find hidden patterns in data.
Combines: Statistics, Mathematics, and Computer Science.
Data Scientist: A professional who analyzes data for insights.
Big Data: Massive volumes of data that cannot be processed with traditional methods.
Key Characteristics: Volume, Variety, Velocity.
Example: Facebook generates petabytes of data daily.
Key Point: Data Science helps organizations use data for a competitive advantage.

slides.title: File-Based vs. Database Approach
content: File-Based: Data stored in separate, isolated files.
Problems: Data duplication, inconsistency, and data isolation.
Example: HR and Finance departments having different employee data.
Database Approach: Data is stored in a single, central repository.
Managed by DBMS software.
Key Point: The Database approach solves the problems of the file-based approach.

slides.title: Advantages of the Database Approach
content: Data Independence: Data is not tied to a single application.
Data Sharing: The database can be accessed by different users.
Avoids Data Redundancy: Data is stored in one place.
Improved Data Security: Data can be accessed only by authorized users.
Key Point: Databases provide efficient, secure, and consistent data management.

slides.title: Basic Data Modeling Concepts
content: Data Model: The blueprint of a database.
Entities: Real-world objects (e.g., Student, Customer, Book).
Attributes: Properties of entities (e.g., Student Name, Customer ID).
Relationships: Associations between entities.
Three Types of Relationships: One-to-One, One-to-Many, Many-to-Many.
Key Point: Data models define the structure and rules for the database.

slides.title: Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD)
content: ERD is a visual representation of a data model.
Components: Entities (Rectangles), Attributes (Ellipses), Relationships (Lines).
Example: A diagram showing Student and Book entities connected by a 'Borrows' relationship.
Key Point: ERD helps communicate database design clearly.

slides.title: Relational Data Model
content: Stores data in two-dimensional tables called 'relations'.
A Table has Rows (Records) and Columns (Fields/Attributes).
Primary Key: A unique identifier for each record.
Foreign Key: A link to the primary key of another table.
Key Point: The relational model is the most widely used data model.

slides.section: 3.3 Creating Relational Database in Microsoft Access
slides.title: Microsoft Access: Tables & Queries
content: Microsoft Access: A relational DBMS software.
Creating a Table: Use 'Design View' to define field names and data types.
Data Types: Text, Number, Date/Time, Currency.
Creating a Query: Use 'Query Design' to retrieve data.
You can add criteria to filter results.
Selecting data from multiple tables: Establish relationships using primary and foreign keys.
Key Point: Access provides the tools to build and manage databases.

slides.title: The Web and its Foundations
content: The Web is a popular service that runs on the Internet.
Invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989.
Four Essential Foundations: HTML, HTTP, Web Server, Web Browser.
HTML: Language for creating webpages.
HTTP: Protocol for communication.
Web Server: Software that stores webpages.
Web Browser: Software to view webpages.
Key Point: The Web is a system for accessing and sharing information over the Internet.

slides.title: Website Design Guidelines
content: Website Design: Planning a website's layout, navigation, and look.
Target Audience: Design for the intended users.
Navigation: Organize pages logically for easy movement.
Consistency: Maintain a uniform look and feel.
Simplicity: Avoid clutter, use colors/graphics effectively.
Accessibility: Ensure the site is usable by everyone, including people with disabilities.
Key Point: Good design focuses on the user experience.

slides.title: HTML Tags, Elements & Document Structure
content: HTML: Markup language for creating webpages.

HTML Tags: Predefined names in angle brackets (e.g.,

,

).

HTML Elements: Start tag, content, end tag (e.g.,

...

).

Void Elements: No end tag (e.g.,
, ).
Document Structure: <!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head> (meta info), <body> (page content).
Key Point: Webpages are built with HTML elements.

slides.title: HTML Attributes, Images & Videos
content: Attributes: Define properties for HTML elements (e.g., align, src).
Inserting Images: .
Inserting Videos: <video src='path/to/video.mp4' controls>.
Video attributes: controls (play/pause), width, height.
Key Point: Attributes provide control over how content is displayed.

slides.title: Creating Hyperlinks
content: Links are created using the <a> (anchor) tag.
Syntax: Clickable Text.
target attribute: Controls where the link opens.
target='_blank': Opens in a new tab.
target='_self': Opens in the same tab.
Images as links: .
Key Point: Links connect webpages and resources.

slides.title: Links to Page Sections
content: Create links to different parts of the same page.
Step 1: Mark a location with <a name='section1'>.
Step 2: Link to it with <a href='#section1'>.
This is useful for large pages to allow quick navigation.
Key Point: This improves user navigation within a long webpage.

slides.title: HTML Tables
content: Tables organize data in rows and columns.
Key tags: <table>, <tr> (row), <th> (header cell), <td> (data cell).
Use the 'border' attribute to add a border.
Merging Cells: colspan (merge columns), rowspan (merge rows).
Tables can be used to create a page layout.
Key Point: Tables are powerful for organizing data and layout.

slides.title: Types of HTML Lists
content: Ordered Lists <ol>: Numbered lists. Use <li> for items.
Unordered Lists <ul>: Bulleted lists. Use <li> for items.
Description Lists <dl>: For term-definition pairs.
<dt> (term) and <dd> (description).
Lists can be nested (one list inside another).
Key Point: Lists are used to present information in a structured way.

slides.title: Basics of Troubleshooting
content: Hardware Troubleshooting: Systematic approach to locating and solving hardware problems.
Start with general issues and get more specific.
Basic checks: Power connection, all cables are secure, devices are turned on.
Important: Always shut down the computer before internal maintenance.
Key Point: Troubleshooting is a step-by-step process of elimination.

slides.title: POST, Beep Codes, and BIOS
content: POST (Power On Self-Test): Diagnoses hardware during startup.
Beep Codes: Sounds indicating specific hardware failures.
No beep, long beeps, short beeps all indicate different problems.
BIOS: Program to start the computer and manage data flow.
CMOS: Chip storing system settings; a CMOS alert means the battery needs replacing.
Key Point: POST and beep codes give early diagnostic clues.

slides.title: Event Viewer and Device Manager
content: Event Viewer: A Windows tool that logs system and application errors.
Provides: The problem, date/time, severity, source, and user.
Device Manager: A Windows utility to check and manage hardware.
Error Icons: Yellow triangle (problem), Red X (disabled/removed), Downward arrow (disabled), Question mark (driver needed).
Key Point: These tools help identify the source of hardware or software problems.

slides.title: Performance Diagnostic Tools
content: Performance Monitor: Gives a quick view of CPU, Memory, Disk, and Network performance.
Task Manager can be used to see this information.
Resource Monitor: Provides an in-depth look at CPU, Network, Memory, and Disk usage.
It helps identify applications that are using excessive resources.
Key Point: These tools help diagnose performance issues.

slides.title: Preventive Maintenance: Dust, Antivirus, Backup
content: Preventive Maintenance: Routine measures to reduce hardware failure.
Dust Cleaning: Using microfiber cloth, chemical cleaners, and vacuum cleaners to clean the case and internal parts.
Antivirus Software: Prevents, detects, and removes malware. Examples: AVAST, AVG, AVIRA.
Backup: Copying data to external storage to recover from data loss.
Key Point: Regular maintenance prevents problems.

slides.title: Disk Defragmentation & Power Protection
content: Disk Fragmentation: Scattering of file parts on the hard drive, slowing performance.
Defragmentation: Reorganizing files to store them contiguously.
Surge Protector: Protects against power surges.
Stabilizer: Provides a consistent voltage level.
Voltage Regulator: Protects against power sags/brownouts.
UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply): A battery that provides short-term power during an outage.
Key Point: Defragmentation improves speed, and power devices prevent damage.

slides.title: Programming Language Levels
content: Machine Language: Low-level language of 1s and 0s. Directly understood by the computer.
Assembly Language: Low-level language using mnemonics. Requires an Assembler to translate.
High-Level Language: Closer to human language. Easier to write.
Translators: Compilers (translate entire program) or Interpreters (translate line by line).
Key Point: High-level languages are easier for programmers.

slides.title: Syntax and Semantics
content: Syntax: The grammatical rules of a programming language.
A program must have correct syntax to run.
Syntax Error: When code violates syntax rules.
Semantics: The meaning of the program's elements.
Logic Error: The program runs but produces incorrect results.
Key Point: Syntax is about form, Semantics is about meaning.

slides.title: Getting Started with Python
content: Python is a popular, easy-to-learn high-level language.
IDLE (Integrated Development and Learning Environment): Python's free IDE.
Interactive Interpreter: Write and execute one line at a time (>>> prompt).
Text Editor: Write and save scripts (files with a .py extension).
print() function: Displays output.
Key Point: Python is accessible and great for beginners.

slides.title: Variables, Identifiers, and Data Types
content: Variables: Memory locations to store data.
Identifiers: Names given to variables (must start with letter or underscore).
Data Types: int (integer), float (floating-point), str (string), bool (True/False).
Assignment Operator (=): Assigns a value to a variable (e.g., x = 5).
Key Point: Variables store data of specific types.

slides.title: Operators and Type Conversion
content: Arithmetic Operators: +, -, *, /, // (floor division), % (modulus), ** (exponent).
Boolean Operators: and, or, not.
Implicit Type Conversion: Python automatically converts data types (e.g., int to float).
Explicit Type Conversion: Programmer uses built-in functions like int(), float(), str().
Key Point: Understanding operators and types is essential for programming.

slides.title: Statements vs. Expressions
content: Statement: An instruction that the interpreter executes (e.g., x=5, print(x)).
Expression: Code that evaluates to a value (e.g., 5, x, x+5).
In the Interactive Interpreter, an expression alone displays its value.
In a script file, the print() function is needed to see the value of an expression.
Key Point: Statements are actions, Expressions are values.

slides.title: Input and Output in Python
content: Programs accept input, process it, and produce output.
input() function: Reads data from the keyboard.
Syntax: variable = input('prompt')
input() always returns a string.
Explicit Conversion: Use int() or float() to convert for math operations.
Example: Program to calculate the area of a circle.
Key Point: Programs interact with the user via input and output.
